Information theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics
OurBigBook.com Words: 20k Articles: 185
Information theory quantifies how much uncertainty messages contain, how efficiently they can be represented, and how reliably they can pass through a noisy channel. Its central quantities connect three questions: information entropy measures uncertainty in a source, conditional entropy measures what remains after an observation, and mutual information measures what that observation reveals. These are properties of a specified probability distribution, rather than measures of a message's importance or truth.
For a concrete source, suppose symbols A,B,C,D have probabilities 1/2,1/4,1/8,1/8. A fixed-length binary representation needs two bits per symbol. Instead assign the prefix code A↦0, B↦10, C↦110, D↦111. Reading from left to right gives an unambiguous decoding because no codeword begins another. The expected value of the length is
21​⋅1+41​⋅2+81​⋅3+81​⋅3=47​.
(1)
This saves an average of 1/4 of a bit per symbol, or 12.5% of the fixed-length representation, with no loss of symbols. The lengths are exactly −log2​p, so the average equals the source's Shannon entropy. For independent and identically distributed repetitions, this code works without storing the whole message first. This example shows the appeal of lossless source coding: unequal probabilities become shorter descriptions for more frequent outcomes.
Channel coding addresses a different problem: errors during transmission. A shorter representation removes predictable structure; an error-correcting representation adds carefully chosen structure that helps recover corrupted symbols. Shannon's source coding theorem and the Shannon second coding theorem identify limits for these respective tasks under their hypotheses. The beauty is that source details and hardware details can meet through a small number of mathematical quantities, notably information entropy and channel capacity.
Claude E. Shannon's A Mathematical Theory of Communication appeared in the Bell System Technical Journal in July and October 1948. Its introduction separates the engineering problem of reproducing messages from their semantic meaning; subsequent sections develop probabilistic source models, noiseless coding, and transmission with noise. It also acknowledges earlier work by Harry Nyquist and Ralph Hartley.[ref]

Bhattacharyya coefficient (B(p,q)=∑i​pi​qi​​)

Words: 125 Articles: 1
Information theory OurBigBook.com
For probability distributions p,q on the same finite alphabet, the Bhattacharyya coefficient measures their square-root overlap:
B(p,q)=∑i​pi​qi​​.
(2)
The vectors (pi​​)i​ and (qi​​)i​ have unit Euclidean norm, so the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives 0≤B≤1. Equality B=1 holds exactly when the distributions agree; B=0 holds exactly when they assign positive probability to disjoint outcomes. For p=(0.9,0.1) and q=(0.6,0.4), B=0.54​+0.2≈0.934847. This overlap is not the probability that two independent draws agree, which here is 0.58.
The fidelity of commuting mixed states reduces to this coefficient. More generally, the measurement characterization of quantum fidelity minimizes it over outcome distributions of a common measurement in quantum mechanics, connecting classical overlap to the unsquared quantum fidelity.

Bhattacharyya distance (DB​(P,Q)=−lnB(P,Q))

Words: 32
Bhattacharyya coefficient OurBigBook.com
The Bhattacharyya distance is the negative natural logarithm of the Bhattacharyya coefficient, with −ln0=∞. It is zero for identical probability distributions and infinite for disjoint probability supports. Despite the name, it need not satisfy the triangle inequality required of a metric.

Communication channel

Words: 38
Information theory OurBigBook.com
A communication channel describes how transmitted inputs become received outputs. In a probabilistic model, conditional probabilities specify which outputs each input can produce. A discrete memoryless channel uses the same finite transition law independently on successive symbols; channel capacity quantifies its optimal reliable transmission rate.

Bit (b∈{0,1})

Words: 48
Information theory OurBigBook.com
A bit is a binary classical symbol with two distinguishable values, zero and one. A uniform random bit has one bit of information entropy, while a biased binary symbol has less. Sending one bit means transmitting one symbol from this binary alphabet; the mutual information it carries about a particular input need not be one.

Nat (unit, nat)

Words: 19
Information theory OurBigBook.com
The unit for information content or information entropy computed with natural logarithms. Converting to bits divides the numerical value by log2, so 1nat=(1/log2)bits.

Memoryless classical information source (p(un)=∏j=1n​p(uj​))

Words: 49
Information theory OurBigBook.com
A memoryless classical source emits independent and identically distributed random variables from a fixed finite alphabet. Its block probability mass function factors as shown, and its information per symbol is the Shannon entropy H(U)=−∑u​p(u)log2​p(u). Zero-probability symbols never occur and contribute zero to the entropy. The typical sequence theorem describes the size and probability of the high-probability block set used for reliable compression.

A finite alphabet is an alphabet whose symbols form a finite set. The binary alphabet {0,1} and a finite vocabulary of possible messages are examples.

Conditional entropy (H(Y∣X))

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Information theory OurBigBook.com
For finite discrete random variables, conditional entropy is the average remaining information entropy of Y after the value of X is known:
H(Y∣X)=∑x:pX​(x)>0​pX​(x)H(Y∣X=x).
(3)
Each observation X=x changes the probability distribution used to describe Y; the average weights that uncertainty by how often the observation occurs. An observation can increase uncertainty for one particular outcome, even though conditioning reduces entropy on average for finite variables.
For example, let Y choose A,B,C,D with probabilities 1/2,1/4,1/8,1/8, and let X report whether Y=A. If it reports yes, there is no remaining uncertainty. Otherwise the conditional probabilities are 1/2,1/4,1/4, whose information entropy is 3/2 bits. The two reports each occur with probability 1/2, so H(Y∣X)=3/4 of a bit. The original uncertainty was 7/4 bits: this observation removes exactly one bit on average.
If Y is a function of X, then H(Y∣X)=0: the observation determines the answer. If X and Y are independent random variables, then H(Y∣X)=H(Y): the observation gives no improvement. These endpoints make conditional entropy useful for separating relevant observations from irrelevant ones. They also lead to the chain rule for information entropy, H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X), which counts the first uncertainty and the remaining uncertainty without double counting.

Equality in the entropy conditioning inequality

Words: 48
Conditional entropy OurBigBook.com
For discrete random variables with finite information entropy H(X), Gibbs inequality gives
H(X)−H(X∣Y)=∑y​pY​(y)D(pX∣y​∥pX​)≥0.
(4)
Equality holds exactly when X and Y are independent random variables. Finiteness matters: if A has infinite information entropy and is independent of a fair bit B, then X=(A,B) and Y=B are dependent but H(X)=H(X∣Y)=+∞.

Chain rule for conditional entropy (H(X,Z∣Y)=H(X∣Y)+H(Z∣X,Y))

Words: 43
Conditional entropy OurBigBook.com
For classical finite random variables, H(X,Z∣Y)=H(X∣Y)+H(Z∣X,Y)=H(Z∣Y)+H(X∣Z,Y). Each identity follows by inserting the corresponding joint entropy into H(X,Z,Y)−H(Y). The two orders are particularly useful when one variable is a deterministic function of the others, as in Fano's inequality via an error indicator.

Conditional entropy under a deterministic change of variables

Words: 39
Conditional entropy OurBigBook.com
If f(x,z) is a bijection of x for every fixed z, then
H(f(X,Z)∣Z)=H(X∣Z).
(5)
In particular, translating a random variable in a finite group by a value determined by the conditioning variable does not change its conditional entropy.

Conditioning reduces entropy (H(X∣Y)≤H(X))

Words: 813 Articles: 4
Conditional entropy OurBigBook.com
For finite discrete random variables X,Y, knowing Y reduces the information entropy of X on average:
H(X∣Y)=∑y:pY​(y)>0​pY​(y)H(X∣Y=y)≤H(X).
(6)
Equality holds exactly when X and Y are independent random variables. The average over observations is essential: H(X∣Y=y) can exceed H(X) for a particular y. All logarithms here have base two, giving bits, and zero-probability terms contribute zero.[ref]
For Bayesian inference, this compares a prior distribution with the posterior distributions produced by possible observations. An unexpected report can make previously unlikely alternatives plausible, while useful reports reduce uncertainty overall. For lossless source coding, an observation shared by encoder and decoder lets them choose descriptions for the appropriate conditional distribution; sending that observation also has a cost. The example below makes both the saving and that cost explicit.
In A Mathematical Theory of Communication by Claude Shannon (1948), the definition of conditional entropy is already an average over observations, followed by the inequality and its independence condition in section 6, property 6. The phrase “knowledge reduces uncertainty” must be read with that averaging convention.[ref]

An observation can increase entropy

Words: 123
Conditioning reduces entropy OurBigBook.com
Consider a binary state X and a report Y with the following joint probability mass function:
X=0X=1pY​(y)​Y=04/504/5​Y=11/101/101/5​pX​(x)9/101/101​​
(7)
Before the report, X=0 is strongly favored: its information entropy is H(X)=h2​(1/10)≈0.468996 bits, where h2​ is binary entropy. A report Y=1 makes the two states equally likely, so H(X∣Y=1)=1 bit, strictly larger than before. This report occurs with probability 1/5. The more common report Y=0 determines X=0, giving H(X∣Y=0)=0. Therefore the averaged conditional entropy is
H(X∣Y)=54​⋅0+51​⋅1=51​<h2​(1/10)=H(X).
(8)
The resulting mutual information is I(X;Y)=h2​(1/10)−1/5≈0.268996 bits. The rare report increases uncertainty about the state; that increase does not make the report useless. Together the reports remove uncertainty on average. These are stipulated probabilities in an exact model, not measured frequencies.

Independent revelation of a binary variable (H(X∣Y)=(1−r)h2​(p),I(X;Y)=rh2​(p))

Words: 275
Conditioning reduces entropy OurBigBook.com
Let X be a Bernoulli random variable with Pr(X=1)=p. Independently of X, a Bernoulli random variable R with Pr(R=1)=r decides whether to reveal it:
Y={X,⊥,​R=1,R=0.​
(9)
The symbol ⊥ means “hidden” and is distinct from both binary states. This is a binary erasure channel with erasure probability 1−r. The hidden report leaves the posterior distribution equal to the prior distribution, because hiding is independent of the state. Either visible report determines X. Weighting these three reports gives the exact conditional entropy and mutual information:
H(X)=h2​(p),H(X∣Y)=(1−r)h2​(p),I(X;Y)=rh2​(p).
(10)
For p=1/4 and r=1/2, H(X)=h2​(1/4)=2−(3/4)log2​3≈0.811278 bits, while H(X∣Y)=I(X;Y)≈0.405639 bits. With r=0 the report tells us nothing; with r=1 it reveals the state completely. If 0<p<1, every positive reveal probability makes the conditioning inequality strict. At p=0 or p=1, the state was already known and every value of r gives equality.
For a Bayesian inference problem, this model distinguishes an uninformative missing report from a decisive observed state. If hiding depended on X, even Y=⊥ could carry mutual information, and the displayed calculation would change. In lossless source coding, suppose both encoder and decoder already know the reveal pattern for repeated independent and identically distributed pairs. Only the hidden states require descriptions. Applying Shannon's source coding theorem to those states gives an asymptotic average rate (1−r)h2​(p) bits per original state. A single hidden state need not have a codeword of that fractional length.
The reveal pattern itself has information entropy H(R)=h2​(r). If that pattern must also be sent, the chain rule for information entropy gives H(R,X)=h2​(r)+h2​(p), since R and X are independent random variables. Equivalently, H(Y)=h2​(r)+rh2​(p) and H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y)=h2​(r)+h2​(p). Thus a saving in the description of X given Y assumes that Y is already available; it is not a free saving in the description of the whole pair.

Additional conditioning reduces entropy (H(X∣Y,Z)≤H(X∣Y))

Words: 101
Conditioning reduces entropy OurBigBook.com
For finite discrete random variables X,Y,Z, retaining Y and also observing Z gives
H(X∣Y)−H(X∣Y,Z)=I(X;Z∣Y)≥0.
(11)
Equality means conditional independence of X and Z given Y. Both sides average over reports; the additional observation is retained alongside Y.[ref]
A short proof of the original inequality uses Kullback-Leibler divergence:
H(X)−H(X∣Y)=I(X;Y)=∑y:pY​(y)>0​pY​(y)D(pX∣Y=y​∥pX​)≥0.
(12)
Gibbs inequality makes each term nonnegative, vanishing exactly when pX∣Y=y​=pX​: independence for every possible report. Applying this within each Y=y and averaging proves the additional-conditioning inequality.[ref]

Conditioning and differential entropy

Words: 144
Conditioning reduces entropy OurBigBook.com
With appropriate probability density functions and finite differential entropies, h(X)−h(X∣Y)=I(X;Y)≥0, with equality iff independence. Differential entropy does not reverse the inequality; infinite or undefined quantities cannot justify subtraction.[ref]
However, differential entropy can be negative and depends on the choice of coordinates. For X with a uniform distribution on an interval of length a>0, h(X)=log2​a; in particular a=1/2 gives −1. Rescaling X by a constant c>0 adds log2​c to both h(X) and h(X∣Y), whenever they are finite, leaving the mutual information unchanged.[ref]
If a continuously distributed X is revealed exactly, its conditional distribution is a Dirac measure with no ordinary probability density function. The discrete identity H(X∣X)=0 has no finite differential entropy counterpart. Mutual information, defined through relative entropy, is infinite here.[ref]

Fano's inequality

Words: 865 Articles: 2
Conditional entropy OurBigBook.com
Fano's inequality turns remaining uncertainty into a constraint on decision errors. If an observation leaves many plausible answers, a decoder cannot usually recover the answer reliably. Its elegant idea is to separate two uncertainties: whether the guess was wrong, and which alternative was correct when it was wrong.
Let X,Y be discrete random variables, with X taking values in a finite alphabet X of cardinality M≥2. Choose any deterministic decoder X=f(Y) whose output lies in X, and define its average error probability pe​=P{X=X}. With base-two logarithms, Fano's inequality states
H(X∣Y)≤h2​(pe​)+pe​log2​(M−1),0≤pe​≤1.
(13)
Here H(X∣Y) is conditional entropy and h2​ is binary entropy, with 0log2​0=0 at the endpoints. Both sides are measured in bits; using natural logarithms throughout gives the same inequality in nats. No uniform source, independence of X,Y, or optimality of the decoder is assumed. Requiring its output to belong to the same alphabet is what leaves at most M−1 alternatives after an error.[ref]
For an exact toy example, give X the discrete uniform distribution on {A,B,C,D}. A channel reports Y=X with probability 1−q and reports each of the other three symbols with probability q/3, where 0≤q≤1. Use the decoder f(y)=y. The output is uniform, and the conditional probabilities after any report y are
P(X=x∣Y=y)={1−q,q/3,​x=y,x=y.​
(14)
Thus pe​=q and direct calculation of the conditional entropy gives
H(X∣Y)=−(1−q)log2​(1−q)−33q​log2​3q​=h2​(q)+qlog2​3.
(15)
This is equality in Fano's inequality for every q∈[0,1]. At q=0.3, each report leaves probabilities (0.7,0.1,0.1,0.1), up to their order, and H(X∣Y)≈1.3568 bits. The two contributions are h2​(0.3)≈0.8813 bits for the error flag and 0.3log2​3≈0.4755 bits for identifying the correct alternative after an error. These are theoretical probabilities, not measured data.
The identity decoder in this example minimizes error only for 0≤q≤3/4: its guessed symbol has the largest posterior probability exactly when 1−q≥q/3. At q=3/4, X,Y are independent random variables and all four guesses tie. For q>3/4, guessing any one of the three other symbols has error probability 1−q/3<q. Equality in Fano's inequality therefore does not certify an optimal decoder.
For usefulness, combine h2​(pe​)≤1 with log2​(M−1)≤log2​M to obtain the simpler consequence
pe​≥max{0,log2​MH(X∣Y)−1​}.
(16)
For a uniform X, H(X∣Y)=log2​M−I(X;Y), so this becomes pe​≥max{0,1−(I(X;Y)+1)/log2​M}. This connects mutual information to unavoidable decision error in channel coding or classification in statistical learning; it can rule out reliable recovery regardless of the chosen decoder.[ref]
The sharper right-hand side FM​(p)=h2​(p)+plog2​(M−1) increases from zero to log2​M on 0≤p≤1−1/M, then decreases: in the interior, FM′​(p)=log2​((M−1)(1−p)/p). When interpreting the inequality by inverting a curve, use its increasing branch to obtain a lower error threshold. A decoder that chooses a largest posterior probability, as in maximum a posteriori decoding, always has pe​≤1−1/M, since the largest of M conditional probabilities is at least 1/M. Arbitrary decoders can have larger error. In particular, low conditional entropy does not force every decoder to work well: with a fair binary X and Y=X, the rule f(Y)=1−Y has pe​=1 even though H(X∣Y)=0. Fano's inequality supplies a constraint, not an exact error prediction for each rule.

Fano's inequality via an error indicator (H(X∣Y)≤h(pe​)+pe​log2​(∣JX​∣−1))

Words: 285
Fano's inequality OurBigBook.com
Under the hypotheses of Fano's inequality, let JX​=X, M=∣JX​∣, and let Z=1{X=f(Y)}​ be the indicator random variable of an error. Its probability of being one is pe​. The h in the displayed bound denotes binary entropy h2​ in bits. Since Z is a deterministic function of (X,Y), H(Z∣X,Y)=0. Applying the chain rule for conditional entropy in both orders gives the exact decomposition
H(X∣Y)​=H(X,Z∣Y)=H(Z∣Y)+H(X∣Z,Y).​
(17)
The first term is bounded by H(Z)=h2​(pe​), because conditioning reduces entropy. For the second term, fix a report Y=y: if Z=0, then X=f(y) is known; if Z=1, then X lies among at most M−1 other symbols. Maximum entropy on a finite alphabet bounds the latter uncertainty by log2​(M−1). Averaging over the reports and the error flag gives
H(X∣Z,Y)≤(1−pe​)⋅0+pe​log2​(M−1).
(18)
This proves Fano's inequality. Events of zero probability contribute zero to this average, so the proof also covers pe​=0,1 without assigning a conditional distribution to an impossible event.[ref]
The decomposition also explains equality. The first bound is exact when the indicator random variable Z and Y are independent random variables: knowing the report does not change the error probability. The second is exact when, for every report with positive error probability, the wrong-symbol conditional distribution is uniform on all M−1 alternatives. Both conditions hold in the four-symbol toy channel of Fano's inequality. At q=0, the second condition is vacuous; at q=1, the flag is constant but three alternatives remain, giving H(X∣Y)=log2​3. For M=2, there is just one alternative after an error, so the second term vanishes: all remaining uncertainty is whether the single alternative must replace the guess.

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Information theory OurBigBook.com
For finite discrete random variables, mutual information is the reduction of information entropy provided by observing the other variable:
I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).
(20)
The last expression makes the symmetry I(X;Y)=I(Y;X) visible. It is nonnegative and is zero exactly when X and Y are independent random variables. One way to see both facts is
I(X;Y)=∑x,y:p(x,y)>0​p(x,y)log2​pX​(x)pY​(y)p(x,y)​=D(pX,Y​∥pX​pY​),
(21)
where D is the Kullback-Leibler divergence with base-two logarithms. The Gibbs inequality gives nonnegativity; equality means that the joint probability distribution factors. The statement extends to more general distributions via relative entropy, but differences of infinite information entropies must not be used as if they were finite numbers.
A binary symmetric channel gives a useful example. Let X be a fair bit, let N be an independent Bernoulli random variable with error probability q, and set Y=X⊕N, where ⊕ is exclusive or. The output is also a fair bit, but knowing the input leaves just the error uncertainty:
H(Y)=1,H(Y∣X)=h2​(q),I(X;Y)=1−h2​(q).
(22)
Here h2​ is binary entropy. At q=0.1, h2​(q)≈0.469, so the output carries about 0.531 bits of mutual information about the input per use. This is an average uncertainty reduction, not a claim that each observed symbol can be divided into fractional physical bits.
At q=1/2, every output is equally likely for either input, so I(X;Y)=0. At q=1, the output is always the inverted input: knowing this rule lets the receiver recover the input exactly, so I(X;Y)=1 again. A high raw error rate need not mean low mutual information when the errors are predictable. For this particular channel the fair input is optimal, giving the binary symmetric channel capacity 1−h2​(q).
Mutual information detects dependence that ordinary correlation can miss. Let X be uniform on {−1,0,1} and Y=X2. Symmetry gives E[X]=E[XY]=0, hence zero covariance and zero correlation, while Y is completely determined by X. Thus I(X;Y)=H(Y)=h2​(1/3)>0. This distinction is useful whenever a relationship is nonlinear: knowing one variable can reveal another without a linear trend.

For a fully computed example, take independent random variables X,Y that are fair bits, and let Z=X⊕Y, where ⊕ is exclusive or. The complete joint probability distribution has only these four positive entries:

Every pair (x,y) has probability 1/4=pX​(x)pY​(y), so I(X;Y)=4(1/4)log2​1=0. But pZ​(0)=pZ​(1)=1/2. Given Z=0, the pairs (0,0),(1,1) each have conditional probability 1/2, while both conditional marginals are fair. Thus

Given Z=1, the pairs (0,1),(1,0) give the same calculation. Therefore

(28)
The conditional entropy calculation tells the same story: H(X∣Z)=1 because either value of Z leaves X fair, whereas H(X∣Y,Z)=0 because X=Y⊕Z. Learning the exclusive or does not reveal either bit alone; it reveals whether they agree, so learning one then determines the other.
This example distinguishes conditional independence from ordinary independence. It also disproves the claim that conditioning always reduces mutual information, despite conditioning reduces entropy. There is no general ordering between I(X;Y∣Z) and I(X;Y): the example above increases it from zero to one, while taking Y=X and Z=X for a fair bit decreases it from one to zero. The chain rule for mutual information explains why both are possible.[ref]
Conditional mutual information is useful for asking whether an additional observation tells us anything after information already available has been accounted for. Its zero case expresses conditional independence exactly; in a Markov chain, this is the step that turns the chain rule for mutual information into the data processing inequality.

Chain rule for mutual information (I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z∣Y))

For finite discrete random variables, the mutual information supplied by two observations equals the information supplied by the first plus the additional conditional mutual information supplied by the second:
I(X;Y,Z)​=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z∣Y)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y∣Z).​
(29)
The order changes the individual contributions but leaves the total unchanged.[ref] To prove the first identity, add and subtract the intermediate conditional entropy:
I(X;Y,Z)​=H(X)−H(X∣Y,Z)=[H(X)−H(X∣Y)]+[H(X∣Y)−H(X∣Y,Z)].​
(30)
With base-two logarithms, all contributions are in bits. Repeatedly inserting intermediate conditional entropies makes them cancel, as in a telescoping series, and gives the rule for any finite list of observations:
I(X;Y1​,…,Yn​)=∑j=1n​I(X;Yj​∣Y1​,…,Yj−1​),
(31)
where the j=1 term is I(X;Y1​). The same calculation with W already known gives I(X;Y,Z∣W)=I(X;Y∣W)+I(X;Z∣Y,W).
For the fair-bit exclusive or example in conditional mutual information, observing Y alone tells nothing about X, but observing Z after Y tells everything:
I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z∣Y)=0+(1−0)=1.
(32)
Here H(X∣Y)=1 by independence and H(X∣Y,Z)=0 because X=Y⊕Z. In the reverse order, H(X∣Z)=1, so I(X;Z)=0 and I(X;Y∣Z)=1: the two observations are individually uninformative but jointly reveal one bit. Simply adding their separate mutual informations would miss all of it.
The chain rule is useful for measuring the value of each new observation without double counting information already supplied. It also guarantees I(X;Y,Z)≥I(X;Y) by nonnegativity of conditional mutual information. Keeping Y and adding Z can help, even though discarding Y and retaining only a processed Z is constrained by the data processing inequality. Equating the two observation orders gives the precise identity
I(X;Y∣Z)−I(X;Y)=I(X;Z∣Y)−I(X;Z),
(33)
which explains why there is no general rule that conditioning decreases mutual information.

Chernoff information measures how quickly repeated independent evidence can distinguish two fixed probability distributions. Suppose a statistical hypothesis test observes n independent and identically distributed random variables, with common law P under one simple hypothesis and Q under the other. Give the two hypotheses fixed positive prior probabilities, and let pn∗​ be the smallest achievable average error probability. For distinct positive probability mass functions on a common finite alphabet,
limn→∞​−n1​lnpn∗​=C(P,Q),C(P,Q)=−min0≤s≤1​ln∑x​P(x)sQ(x)1−s.
(63)
Here ln is the natural logarithm, so the error exponent is measured in nats per observation. This optimal rate is unchanged by choosing different fixed positive prior probabilities; the best decision rule and finite-sample error can still change.[ref]
The interpretation is pn∗​=exp(−nC(P,Q)+o(n)): a larger Chernoff information means fewer observations are needed at the leading exponential scale. It does not assert the exact finite-sample identity pn∗​=e−nC(P,Q). The finite-sample Chernoff error bound and the explicit Chernoff information for complementary Bernoulli distributions make this distinction concrete. This is useful when designing repeated measurements or comparing sensors whose output probability distributions differ under two candidate conditions.
For probability mass functions with zero entries, define the affinity for 0<s<1 and use C(P,Q)=−lninf0<s<1​∑x​P(x)sQ(x)1−s, taking endpoint limits when needed. This avoids an ambiguous 00 convention. Identical laws give C=0; disjoint probability supports give C=∞, because one observation separates them perfectly. The displayed finite-rate theorem concerns fixed laws with common positive support, not laws that change with n or arbitrarily dependent repeated observations.

Total correlation (TC(X1​,…,Xn​))

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Information theory OurBigBook.com
Total correlation measures how much dependence is lost when a joint probability distribution is replaced by the product of its marginal probability distributions. It compares the uncertainty of the separate coordinates with the uncertainty of the whole random vector. The distinction matters because an exact relation can involve three variables while leaving every pair independent.
For random variables X1​,…,Xn​ with finite alphabets, define
TC(X1​,…,Xn​)=i=1∑n​H(Xi​)−H(X1​,…,Xn​)=D(PX1​,…,Xn​​​i=1⨂n​PXi​​).​
(70)
Here H is information entropy, the entropy of the full random vector is joint entropy, and D is relative entropy. Base-two logarithms give bits; natural logarithms give nats. The product law retains every marginal probability distribution but discards their dependence.[ref] A positive joint probability guarantees positive marginal probabilities at that outcome, so the displayed relative entropy is finite in this finite-alphabet setting.
For two variables, total correlation is exactly mutual information. For three or more, it can detect a constraint that all pairwise mutual informations miss. Relative entropy nonnegativity gives TC≥0, with equality exactly when the coordinates are jointly independent random variables.
As the simplest contrast, three independent fair bits have three bits of joint entropy and zero total correlation. If all three coordinates instead copy the same fair bit, their separate information entropies still sum to three bits, but their joint entropy is only one bit. Their total correlation is therefore two bits. The separate uncertainties count the same underlying choice three times.

Parity constraint and total correlation (Z=X⊕Y,TC(X,Y,Z)=1 bit)

Words: 445 Articles: 1
Total correlation OurBigBook.com
Let X,Y be independent fair bits and set Z=X⊕Y, their exclusive or. The four possible triples are 000,011,101,110, each with probability 1/4. Every coordinate is fair, and every pair has all four outcomes with equal probability. Thus each pair's mutual information is zero, as in pairwise independence does not imply joint independence.
The full random vector has joint entropy log2​4=2 bits, while the marginal information entropies sum to three bits. Consequently
TC(X,Y,Z)=3−2=1 bit.​
(71)
The product of the marginals predicts probability 1/8 for every triple, including the four impossible ones. On each possible triple, the ratio of true to product probability is (1/4)/(1/8)=2; averaging its base-two logarithm gives the same one bit of relative entropy.
The example gives a concrete use for joint information measures. A lossless source coding scheme that treats the three coordinates separately needs three bits here. If the decoder knows the integer parity rule, the encoder can send just X,Y and let the decoder reconstruct Z exactly. Pairwise independence does not reveal that saving. This is a stipulated source law and an explicit two-bit code, rather than a promise that arbitrary data can be shortened.

Noisy parity total correlation (TC(X,Y,Z)=1−h2​(ε))

Words: 284
Parity constraint and total correlation OurBigBook.com
Keep X,Y as independent fair bits, introduce an independent Bernoulli random variable N with P(N=1)=ε, and set Z=X⊕Y⊕N. The extra bit flips the integer parity rule with probability ε. For each even-integer parity triple the probability is (1−ε)/4; for each odd-integer parity triple it is ε/4.
Every coordinate remains fair, and every pair remains independent for every 0≤ε≤1. For example, after fixing X, the fair independent Y makes Y⊕N fair regardless of ε. A pair's joint probability distribution therefore does not change as noise destroys the three-way relation.
Knowing X,Y, uncertainty in Z is exactly the uncertainty in N. The chain rule for information entropy gives
H(X,Y,Z)=H(X,Y)+H(Z∣X,Y)=2+h2​(ε),
(72)
where h2​ is binary entropy. Hence
TC(X,Y,Z)=1−h2​(ε).​
(73)
At ε=1/4, the result is approximately 0.188722 bits, although all three pairwise mutual informations are zero. At ε=1/2, all eight triples have probability 1/8, giving joint independence and zero total correlation. At ε=1, the complementary integer parity rule is deterministic again, so total correlation returns to one bit.
The example distinguishes "there is a dependence" from "a pair reveals it." Once X,Y are known together, Z is predictable at zero noise; knowing either one alone leaves a fair bit. Total correlation detects the joint departure from independence, but does not by itself specify which variables cause which others.

For finite alphabets, expanding joint entropy with the chain rule for information entropy gives
TC(X1​,…,Xn​)=∑i=2n​[H(Xi​)−H(Xi​∣X1​,…,Xi−1​)]=∑i=2n​I(Xi​;X1​,…,Xi−1​).
(74)
Each term is mutual information with an entire preceding block, rather than necessarily with one preceding variable. Changing the order changes these individual terms but leaves their sum unchanged.
For the noiseless parity constraint and total correlation, I(Y;X)=0 and I(Z;X,Y)=1 bit. The conditional block term supplies exactly the dependence that the pairwise comparisons missed. For three identical copies of a fair bit, the two block terms are both one bit. Thus total correlation counts total departure from the product law, not merely the presence of a single irreducible multiway relation.

Let P be a joint probability distribution on a finite product alphabet, with marginals Pi​. Compare it with a product model Q=⨂i​Qi​, assuming Qi​(xi​)>0 wherever Pi​(xi​)>0. Adding and subtracting the logarithm of ∏i​Pi​(xi​) gives
D(P∥Q)=TC(P)+i∑​D(Pi​∥Qi​).​

The first term is the unavoidable error from discarding dependence; the other terms are errors in the individual marginal probability distributions. Averaging a term that depends only on xi​ under P is the same as averaging it under Pi​, which proves the identity directly.
Among product laws, the choice Qi​=Pi​ minimizes this relative entropy, leaving exactly total correlation. The related cross-entropy equals entropy plus relative entropy identity interprets this as extra average logarithmic loss from using the independent model. It is a statement about a specified joint law and loss function, not a claim that fitting a finite sample automatically recovers that law.

Scope and scale of total correlation

Words: 104
Total correlation OurBigBook.com
For finite alphabets, H(X1​,…,Xn​)≥maxi​H(Xi​), so
0≤TC(X1​,…,Xn​)≤∑i​H(Xi​)−maxi​H(Xi​).
(76)
For n identical copies of one fair bit, the upper bound is attained and total correlation is n−1 bits. Adding another copy increases the result without introducing a new underlying random choice. The choice of coordinates and their grouping therefore matters when comparing systems of different sizes.
For more general random variables, the relative entropy against the product of the marginals supplies a definition of total correlation that may be infinite. Subtracting differential entropies is justified only when those quantities are finite and the entropy identity is valid; an undefined difference of infinities is not a definition. The finite-alphabet examples above avoid that problem entirely.

The abstract of Information Theoretical Analysis of Multivariate Correlation by Satosi Watanabe (1960, printed p. 66) names the sum of individual information entropies minus joint entropy "total correlation." It presents this as the finest grouping of the variables and identifies applications to geometric pattern recognition and shuffling cards marked zero or one. The name therefore connects the uncertainty of a system with the structure linking its parts; the worked integer parity and noisy-integer parity models here are separate examples calculated from their stated laws.

Type (information theory, q​xn​)

Words: 2k Articles: 17
Information theory OurBigBook.com
A type summarizes a string by how often each symbol occurs. Fix a finite alphabet A of cardinality m and a positive length n. For a string xn=(x1​,…,xn​), its empirical distribution is the probability mass function
q​xn​(a)=n#{j:xj​=a}​,a∈A.
(77)
The empirical distribution forgets order. The strings 0011 and 1010 both assign probability 1/2 to each binary symbol; 0001 assigns 3/4 to zero and 1/4 to one. Thus a long string can have a short summary even though that summary does not reconstruct the original order.
For independent and identically distributed symbols, this loss of order has a useful consequence: all strings with the same empirical distribution have the same probability. The method of types uses this symmetry to turn questions about exponentially many strings into counting questions about relatively few frequency profiles.[ref]

Type class (Tn​(q))

Words: 311 Articles: 2
Type (information theory) OurBigBook.com
The type class Tn​(q) contains all length-n strings with empirical distribution q. Each nq(a) must be a nonnegative integer and the counts must sum to n; otherwise the class is empty. Distinct type classes partition An: every string belongs to exactly one class.
For four binary symbols there are five type classes, indexed by the number k of ones. Their cardinalities are 1,4,6,4,1, which sum to 16=24. The balanced class contains exactly 0011,0101,0110,1001,1010,1100. These are six different strings, not six different empirical distributions.

Write na​=nq(a). Arranging na​ copies of each symbol gives the multinomial coefficient
∣Tn​(q)∣=∏a∈A​na​!n!​.​
(78)
The division by the factorials removes permutations among identical copies. In the balanced four-symbol example, ∣T4​(q)∣=4!/(2!2!)=6. For binary symbols this becomes the binomial coefficient (kn​); for three symbols with counts (2,1,1), the class contains 4!/(2!1!1!)=12 strings.

Indexing within a type class

Words: 149
Type class OurBigBook.com
If a decoder already knows the length, alphabet and empirical distribution, it only needs to distinguish ∣Tn​(q)∣ possible strings. A fixed-length index therefore needs ⌈log2​∣Tn​(q)∣⌉ bits. List the six balanced four-symbol strings in increasing lexicographic order and number them 0 through 5. A three-bit index identifies any one of them, whereas writing the original binary string directly takes four bits.
Knowing the empirical distribution is essential to that calculation. If it must also be sent, a simple fixed-length description of which of the five classes was used costs another ⌈log2​5⌉=3 bits. That naive balanced-string message totals six bits and is longer than the raw four-bit string. The example demonstrates the benefit of shared constraints, rather than a free lossless source coding scheme for every input. For long strings over a fixed alphabet, the overhead for identifying a class grows only logarithmically with length, while the information entropy of its frequency profile controls the leading cost within the class.

Method of types

Words: 2k Articles: 13
Type (information theory) OurBigBook.com
The method of types combines two facts: there are few possible empirical distributions, and strings within each type class are equiprobable under an independent and identically distributed source. Information entropy determines how many strings share a frequency profile; relative entropy determines how unlikely that profile is under a specified source law. The connection is useful both for lossless source coding and for understanding rare observations.
The following formulas use natural logarithms, so information entropy and relative entropy are measured in nats. Define
He​(q)=−∑a​q(a)lnq(a),De​(q∥p)=∑a​q(a)lnp(a)q(a)​.
(79)
Here p is the source probability mass function and q is an attainable empirical distribution. Use 0ln0=0; first assume every p(a)>0. Base-two logarithms give the equivalent formulas with 2nH2​(q) and 2−nD2​(q∥p).

Number of empirical types ((m−1n+m−1​))

Words: 126
Method of types OurBigBook.com
A possible empirical distribution corresponds to nonnegative integer counts (n1​,…,nm​) with sum n. Stars and bars therefore gives
#{length-n types}=(m−1n+m−1​)≤(n+1)m.
(80)
The bound also follows by letting each count independently range from zero to n, which overcounts tuples whose sum is wrong. With the alphabet fixed, the count grows polynomially in n, whereas there are mn strings when m≥2. For binary symbols there are exactly n+1 profiles: the number of ones can be any integer from zero through n.
This reduces a rare-event calculation to a sum over profiles when the event depends only on counts. An event that depends on order may instead require counting the relevant subset inside each type class. A source with statistical dependence need not make strings of the same empirical distribution equiprobable; the memoryless assumption cannot simply be dropped.

(n+1)−menHe​(q)≤∣Tn​(q)∣≤enHe​(q).

The upper bound has a short explanation. Under an independent and identically distributed source whose law is q itself, each string in Tn​(q) has probability e−nHe​(q). Multiplying by the number of such strings cannot give a probability above one. A corresponding polynomial lower bound follows from the multinomial coefficient; the Stirling's approximation gives sharper prefactors when needed.
For the balanced four-symbol class, He​(q)=ln2, so the upper bound is e4ln2=16, while the exact size is six. Information entropy is not an exact count for a short string. On the leading scale it becomes precise: the difference divided by n tends to zero as n grows with the alphabet fixed.

Information projection (q∗=argminq∈C​D(q∥p))

Words: 997 Articles: 7
Method of types OurBigBook.com
An information projection chooses the probability distribution that satisfies a constraint while departing least from a reference law in relative entropy. The constraint might specify an expected value, several marginal probability distributions, or another convex set of permissible laws. The reference is held fixed: the variable is the first argument of D(q∥p). Reversing the arguments gives a different minimization problem.
For a finite alphabet A, take a positive reference probability mass function p(a)>0 and a nonempty closed convex set C in the probability simplex. Then
q∗=argq∈Cmin​D(q∥p),D(q∥p)=a:q(a)>0∑​q(a)lnp(a)q(a)​.​
(86)
The minimum exists and its minimizing probability distribution is unique. In this article, natural logarithms give nats. Using base-two logarithms rescales the objective without changing the minimizer.[ref]
If p already meets the constraint, its information projection is p itself by relative entropy nonnegativity. If not, a constraint can change the relative weights of outcomes without specifying every weight individually. Relative entropy minimization under a mean constraint gives an especially useful example: it tilts the reference law rather than choosing an arbitrary distribution with the right average.

Write the three probabilities in outcome order as (q−​,q0​,q+​). The mean constraint is q+​−q−​=1/2, while normalization requires q−​+q0​+q+​=1.
These conditions leave a whole line of possible probability distributions:
q=(x,1/2−2x,1/2+x),0≤x≤1/4.

Take independent and identically distributed draws from the uniform three-outcome reference above. An observed sample mean at least 1/2 is unusual because the source expected value is zero. For two draws, the only successful ordered pairs are (0,1),(1,0),(1,1), giving probability 3/9=1/3.
For long samples, the relevant empirical distributions have mean at least 1/2. The method of types assigns a profile q a leading probability cost e−nD(q∥p). The least costly admissible profile is the information projection on three outcomes: in this example the minimizing mean is on the boundary 1/2, and the leading exponent is approximately 0.197378 nats per draw. The exponential scale is not an exact finite-sample probability formula.[ref]
The attraction of this connection is that a constrained optimization problem predicts the most probable way an unusual aggregate observation can occur. It links relative entropy, expected value constraints and rare empirical distributions without identifying a rare event with just one exact attainable type class.

Rate-distortion theory

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Information theory OurBigBook.com
Rate-distortion theory asks how much mutual information must survive when a representation may lose detail. Lossy compression groups different inputs into one reconstruction; a distortion measure specifies which differences matter. The rate-distortion function then gives a quantitative tradeoff between allowed expected distortion and the required number of bits. A smaller file is useful only if its reconstruction retains the distinctions that the application needs.

Rate-distortion function (R(D))

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Rate-distortion theory OurBigBook.com
Fix a finite source alphabet X, a probability mass function pX​, a finite reconstruction alphabet X, and a nonnegative distortion measure d(x,x^). The information rate-distortion function is
R(D)=infpX∣X​:E[d(X,X)]≤D​I(X;X).
(95)
The source probability distribution stays fixed; the conditional distribution of the reconstruction is what we optimize. Each feasible test channel must keep expected distortion at most D. The objective is mutual information, measured in bits when the logarithms have base two. If no test channel satisfies the constraint, the infimum is +∞.[ref]
Consider independent and identically distributed fair bits and Hamming distortion, which charges one for an incorrect bit. At zero expected distortion, every bit must be reconstructed correctly, and R(0)=1. If an average fraction D=1/4 of incorrect bits is allowed, the binary rate-distortion function gives
R(1/4)=1−h2​(1/4)≈0.18872 bits per source symbol.​
(96)
Here h2​ is binary entropy. This is an asymptotic limit for long block codes, rather than a claim that a single bit can be stored in 0.18872 physical bits. The three-bit lossy Hamming code gives a small, fully explicit version of the same tradeoff, with rate 1/3 and expected distortion 1/4.
Rate-distortion theory separates the question of what is possible from the design of a practical encoder and decoder. It also forces the fidelity criterion to be explicit. Hamming distortion treats all symbol mismatches alike; mean squared error instead penalizes larger numerical errors more strongly. Those objectives can favor different reconstructions of the same data. An average error criterion does not by itself control the error on every individual input.
Claude Shannon's Coding Theorems for a Discrete Source With a Fidelity Criterion by Claude Shannon was published in 1959. Its formulation fixes a cost for replacing one source letter by another and studies the communication rate compatible with the allowed average cost. The important shift is to quantify which distinctions may be discarded, rather than requiring exact recovery of every letter.[ref]

A distortion measure assigns a nonnegative cost to replacing a source symbol x by a reconstruction x^. It need not be a metric: the two alphabets may differ, and neither symmetry nor the triangle inequality is required. Choosing the cost is part of the model. For numerical symbols, d(x,x^)=(x−x^)2 gives mean squared error after averaging; for exact symbol agreement, use Hamming distortion.
Reconstruction alphabet (X)
Words: 32

The reconstruction alphabet is the set of values that the decoder may output. It need not equal the source alphabet. A restricted reconstruction alphabet can prevent zero expected distortion, even if the representation is allowed arbitrarily many bits.
Expected distortion (E[d(X,X)])

Distortion measure (information theory) OurBigBook.com
Expected distortion is the expectation of the reconstruction cost under the joint probability distribution of X and X. It weights common source outcomes more strongly than rare ones. A bound on expected distortion is therefore different from a bound on the cost for every input, or on the probability of exceeding a specified cost.

Distortion measure (information theory) OurBigBook.com
For a block code, separable distortion is the average of the individual symbol costs. With Hamming distortion it is the fraction of incorrectly reconstructed symbols, rather than the unnormalized number of mismatches. This normalization makes expected distortion comparable across different block lengths.[ref]

Rate-distortion function OurBigBook.com
A test channel is a proposed conditional distribution of a reconstruction given the source symbol. It describes a candidate joint probability distribution for evaluating mutual information and expected distortion. It need not be a physical transmission channel, or an implementable one-symbol encoder; the Shannon rate-distortion theorem relates this optimization to long block codes.

Hamming distortion (d(x,x^)=1{x=x^}​)

Words: 397 Articles: 2
Rate-distortion function OurBigBook.com
Hamming distortion is zero for a correctly reconstructed symbol and one for a mismatch. Its expected distortion is the symbol-error probability:
E[d(X,X)]=P(X=X).
(97)
For strings of length n, separable distortion divides their Hamming distance by n. Thus 001 reconstructed as 000 has Hamming distance one and average Hamming distortion 1/3. Counting only whether the whole string is correct would give a different criterion.
Three-bit lossy Hamming code (R=1/3,D=1/4)
Words: 204
Hamming distortion OurBigBook.com
Let X1​,X2​,X3​ be independent fair bits. The encoder sends their majority bit: zero when at least two inputs are zero, and one otherwise. The decoder reconstructs 000 or 111 by repeating that received bit three times. This is lossy compression: different original strings deliberately share a reconstruction.
There are eight equally likely inputs. The strings 000 and 111 have zero Hamming distance from their reconstructions; each of the other six has Hamming distance one. One transmitted bit represents three source symbols, so
R=31​,D=8⋅32⋅0+6⋅1​=41​.​
(98)
Every input has average Hamming distortion at most 1/3, whereas the population average is 1/4. The actual block code therefore obeys R≥R(D)≈0.18872, but does not reach the optimal long-block rate.
This construction uses the same reconstruction strings as the threefold binary repetition code, but the tasks differ. An error-correcting encoder expands one source bit into three transmitted bits; this lossy compression example compresses three source bits into one transmitted bit. The source distribution and the direction of the mapping matter.

For a stationary source of independent and identically distributed fair bits, with Hamming distortion and binary reconstruction alphabet,
R(D)={1−h2​(D),0,​0≤D≤1/2,D≥1/2.​​
(99)
The binary entropy convention is 0log2​0=0. Once D≥1/2, always reconstructing zero meets the distortion constraint without sending any bits. The formula 1−h2​(D) must not be extended to D>1/2: a looser constraint cannot increase the required rate.[ref]
The short argument identifies both sides of the optimum. For any feasible binary reconstruction, put E=X⊕X, using exclusive or. Knowing X makes X and E determine one another, so the conditional entropy obeys
H(X∣X)=H(E∣X)≤H(E)=h2​(P(E=1))≤h2​(D)
(100)
when 0≤D≤1/2. The last step uses the increase of binary entropy on that interval. Hence I(X;X)=1−H(X∣X)≥1−h2​(D). Conversely, choose X=X⊕N with an independent Bernoulli random variable N of parameter D. This binary symmetric channel has expected distortion D and mutual information 1−h2​(D), attaining the bound.

Fixed-length lossy code (Rn​=n−1log2​Mn​)

Words: 60
Rate-distortion function OurBigBook.com
A fixed-length lossy code maps a block of n source symbols to one of Mn​ messages, then maps that message to a reconstruction block. The encoder and decoder together define the reconstruction. Its rate is log2​Mn​/n bits per source symbol; an implementation using a fixed binary message needs ⌈log2​Mn​⌉ transmitted bits per block. Its performance also depends on expected distortion, block length, and the chosen distortion measure.

Shannon's rate-distortion theorem

Words: 149
Rate-distortion function OurBigBook.com
For a finite alphabet source with independent and identically distributed symbols, a finite reconstruction alphabet, and a bounded nonnegative separable distortion, the rate-distortion function is the asymptotic limit for fixed-length lossy codes. In particular, for a distortion target in the interior of the feasible range and every ε>0, sufficiently long block codes exist with rate at most R(D)+ε and expected distortion at most D+ε. Every such n-symbol code obeys Rn​≥R(Dn​), where Dn​ is its actual expected distortion.[ref]
The outline is instructive. The data processing inequality bounds the mutual information in a reconstruction by the information entropy of the transmitted message, which is at most log2​Mn​. Independence and the convexity of the rate-distortion function then give the per-symbol lower bound. For achievability, choose many reconstruction blocks using a suitable probability distribution, so that the source's typical blocks are likely to have an acceptable nearby reconstruction. This is a covering argument; it does not require recovering the original block exactly.

Zero-rate distortion threshold (Dzero​=minx^​E[d(X,x^)])

Words: 82
Rate-distortion function OurBigBook.com
For the finite alphabets considered here, the zero-rate distortion threshold is the smallest expected distortion obtainable by always outputting one fixed reconstruction. Such a reconstruction is independent of the source, so its mutual information is zero. A randomized output that is independent of the source averages the costs of fixed reconstructions and cannot improve their minimum. Thus R(D)=0 exactly when D≥Dzero​. For a fair bit under Hamming distortion, Dzero​=1/2; for a Bernoulli random variable of parameter p, it is min{p,1−p}. The threshold depends on the source probability distribution, rather than only the alphabet.

Channel capacity (C=maxPX​​I(X;Y))

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Information theory OurBigBook.com
Channel capacity is the best reliable information rate available through a specified communication channel. For a discrete memoryless channel with finite input and output alphabets, fixed transition probabilities W(y∣x), and no input-cost constraint, it is
C=maxPX​​I(X;Y)
(101)
in bits per channel use, when the mutual information uses base-two logarithms. The maximization varies the input probability distribution, while keeping the communication channel fixed. A large input alphabet or a large output information entropy alone does not determine how much information gets through: the receiver needs information about the input, rather than merely unpredictable output.
The operational meaning comes from the Shannon second coding theorem. A block code represents one of M possible messages by a word of length n, giving a rate log2​M/n bits per use. Take the message label from the uniform distribution on a finite set of those M choices when measuring average decoding-error probability. For every fixed rate R<C, there are sequences of such block codes whose decoding-error probability tends to zero as n grows; a rate above C cannot have vanishing decoding-error probability. This is an asymptotic limit, rather than a promise that an arbitrary finite block code at a rate below C works well. See MIT 18.310, Shannon's Noisy Coding Theorem, sections 1–2.
For a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p=0.1, the binary symmetric channel capacity is approximately 0.53100441 bits per use. Thus a binary code rate R=1/2 lies below the limit, while R=3/4 lies above it. At R=1/2, two transmitted symbols represent one message bit on average; the redundancy helps distinguish messages after noise. This does not split individual physical symbols into fractional pieces.
The result is useful because it separates two tasks. Computing channel capacity establishes the target imposed by the transition probabilities; constructing an effective block code attempts to approach that target with acceptable delay and decoding effort. The surprise is that reliability can improve indefinitely without forcing every positive rate to disappear. In his 1948 paper, Shannon defines noisy channel capacity in section 12 and develops its operational significance in section 13, Theorem 11. His original formulation uses information per unit time; the fixed-duration channel-use convention here expresses the same rate question per symbol. [ref].

Weakly symmetric channel capacity (C=log2​m−H(one row))

Words: 847 Articles: 5
Channel capacity OurBigBook.com
For a discrete memoryless channel with m output symbols, suppose every row of the transition matrix is a permutation of every other row and all column sums agree. Such a communication channel has
C=log2​m−H(one row).
(102)
The row Shannon entropy is the same for every input, so H(Y∣X) has that fixed value for every input probability distribution. The remaining term H(Y) is at most log2​m by maximum entropy on a finite alphabet.
A uniform input attains the bound. If there are ℓ input symbols, the total of all transition probabilities in the matrix is ℓ; equal column sums must therefore each be ℓ/m. Multiplication by the uniform input mass 1/ℓ gives output mass 1/m in each column. Hence H(Y)=log2​m, which proves the displayed formula. The cyclic ternary channel capacity, binary symmetric channel capacity, and ternary symmetric channel capacity are concrete applications of this symmetry calculation.

Cyclic ternary channel capacity (C=log2​3−h2​(q))

Words: 75
Weakly symmetric channel capacity OurBigBook.com
A discrete memoryless channel on the additive group Z/3Z maps x to x with probability 1−q and to x+1 with probability q. Every input gives the same conditional entropy h2​(q), whereas the output Shannon entropy is at most log2​3. A uniform input produces a uniform output since every column of the transition matrix sums to one. Hence the channel capacity is log2​3−h2​(q) bits per use. This cyclic-error channel differs from a channel distributing its error probability equally over both other output symbols.

Binary symmetric channel capacity (C=1−h2​(p))

Words: 634 Articles: 2
Weakly symmetric channel capacity OurBigBook.com
A binary symmetric channel independently flips each transmitted bit with crossover probability p. Its channel capacity is
C=1−h2​(p),0≤p≤1,
(103)
in bits per use, where h2​ is binary entropy and the endpoint convention is 0log2​0=0. Knowing the input leaves just the uncertainty of the flip, so H(Y∣X)=h2​(p) for every input probability distribution. Since the output is a bit, H(Y)≤1, and thus I(X;Y)≤1−h2​(p). A fair input produces a fair output and reaches the bound. This is the two-symbol case of weakly symmetric channel capacity; Eytan Modiano, MIT 16.36, Channel Capacity and Coding, slides 4–5 gives this calculation.
For crossover probabilities p=0.01,0.1,0.25, the resulting channel capacities are approximately 0.91920686, 0.53100441, and 0.18872188 bits per use. At p=0, the communication channel is noiseless; at p=1/2, the output is independent of the input and the capacity is zero. At p=1, every bit is inverted, a known reversible rule, and capacity is one again. More generally C(p)=C(1−p), because inverting every received bit exchanges the two crossover probabilities. The existing mutual information figure shows this full symmetric curve.
An uncoded transmission illustrates why the raw bit-error probability is not itself channel capacity. At p=0.1, transmitting 100 uncoded bits succeeds on all of them with probability 0.9100≈0.00002656. The probability of at least one error is therefore approximately 0.99997344. A suitable block code changes which received words count as recoverable evidence of a message; simply repeating uncoded transmission at rate one does not obtain the reliability promised at rates below C.

Pr(Y=1)=(1−q)p+q(1−p)=p+(1−2p)q.
(104)
Consequently its mutual information is
I(X;Y)=h2​(p+(1−2p)q)−h2​(p).

Here p specifies the noise and q specifies the input bias; they are different choices. At p=0.1 and q=0.2, the output has Pr(Y=1)=0.26, giving H(Y)≈0.82674637 and I(X;Y)≈0.35775078 bits. With the same noise and the fair input q=1/2, the output becomes fair and I(X;Y)≈0.53100441 bits, attaining binary symmetric channel capacity.
For p=1/2, binary entropy reaches one only at output mass 1/2, and the equation p+(1−2p)q=1/2 forces q=1/2. Thus the maximizing input is unique in those cases. For p=1/2, every input produces the same fair output and zero mutual information, so every input bias is optimal and none transmits information. A fixed input q=0 or q=1 also carries zero mutual information for every p: noise can make its output unpredictable without creating an unknown message to recover.
Flips versus erasures in a binary channel
Words: 216
Binary symmetric channel capacity OurBigBook.com
A binary erasure channel marks its failed transmissions with a special output symbol, whereas a binary symmetric channel changes a bit without announcing whether it changed. At the same nominal failure probability p=0.1, the two communication channels therefore leave different uncertainty. With a fair input, an unerased output determines the input exactly, while the erasure flag leaves one bit of conditional entropy. Thus H(X∣Y)=p and I(X;Y)=1−p=0.9 for the binary erasure channel. This is the binary case of capacity of a finite-alphabet erasure channel.
For the binary symmetric channel at p=0.1, neither possible received symbol rules out either input, and H(X∣Y)=h2​(0.1)≈0.46899559. Its channel capacity is only 1−h2​(0.1)≈0.53100441. A receiver benefits from knowing where information was lost, even when the fraction of affected transmissions is the same.
This comparison concerns the specified transition probabilities, rather than a general ordering of every error mechanism. In particular, at p=1, an erasure flag conveys no input information, while deterministic inversion still conveys a full bit. Reporting only an error percentage loses the distinction between hidden corruption, announced loss, and a predictable reversible transformation.

Information entropy (H(X))

Words: 4k Articles: 36
Information theory OurBigBook.com
For a finite discrete random variable with probability mass function p, its information entropy is the expected value of its information content:
H(X)=−∑x:p(x)>0​p(x)log2​p(x)=E[−log2​p(X)].
(107)
Base-two logarithms give bits; choosing a different base rescales the units. The convention 0log2​0=0 is justified by a limit, so outcomes of zero probability contribute nothing. The definition also applies to countable distributions, but the sum may be infinite.
A fair bit has H=1. A certain outcome has H=0. A Bernoulli random variable that is one with probability 0.1 has H=h2​(0.1)≈0.469 bits, because most of its outcomes are predictable. A rare outcome still has large information content: the outcome of probability 0.1 contributes −log2​(0.1)≈3.322 bits of surprise when it occurs. Entropy is the average surprise, rather than the surprise of each outcome.
For m possible outcomes, 0≤H(X)≤log2​m, with the upper bound attained exactly by the uniform distribution on a finite set. The Gibbs inequality proves this by comparing p with the uniform distribution: D(p∥u)=log2​m−H(X)≥0. Thus increasing predictability reduces the required average description length. The four-symbol prefix code in information theory attains H=7/4 bits exactly; for general probabilities, integer codeword lengths prevent such a perfect match for every individual symbol. Shannon's source coding theorem explains how coding sufficiently long independent blocks approaches the entropy per symbol.
The logarithm is especially natural because independent outcomes have additive surprise: −log2​(pq)=−log2​p−log2​q. Taking expected values gives additive information entropy for independent random variables; for dependent ones, the chain rule for information entropy replaces the second term by conditional entropy. This is why the same quantity can govern both a single observation and a long message.

Information entropy OurBigBook.com
Joint entropy is the information entropy of an entire random vector, treating its coordinates together as one outcome. For random variables with finite alphabets and joint probability mass function p,
H(X1​,…,Xn​)=−∑x1​,…,xn​:p(x1​,…,xn​)>0​p(x1​,…,xn​)log2​p(x1​,…,xn​).
(108)
It is measured in bits. The distinction from separate information entropies is whether shared uncertainty is counted once or repeatedly. Two copies of the same fair bit have joint entropy one bit, since only 00 and 11 can occur. Two independent fair bits have joint entropy two bits, since all four pairs are possible and equiprobable.
For a less symmetric example, assign probabilities 1/2,1/4,1/4 to (X,Y)=(0,0),(1,0),(1,1) respectively. Then
H(X,Y)=21​⋅1+41​⋅2+41​⋅2=23​ bits.​

Here X is fair, while P(Y=1)=1/4. Thus H(X)=1 and H(Y)=h2​(1/4)≈0.811278 bits, where h2​ is binary entropy. Adding the separate information entropies would give approximately 1.811278 bits, overcounting by the mutual information I(X;Y)≈0.311278 bits.
The chain rule for information entropy makes the shared information explicit:
H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X).
(110)
In this example Y is certain given X=0 and fair given X=1, so its average conditional entropy is H(Y∣X)=21​⋅0+21​⋅1=1/2 bit. Sending the first coordinate changes how much uncertainty remains in the second. A prefix code with codewords 0, 10, 11 for the three possible pairs has average length 3/2 bits, exactly the joint entropy in this stipulated law.
For finite alphabets,
maxi​H(Xi​)≤H(X1​,…,Xn​)≤∑i​H(Xi​).
(111)
The lower bound follows because knowing the full random vector determines every coordinate; the upper bound follows from conditioning reduces entropy in the chain rule for information entropy. Equality in the upper bound means joint independence. The difference from that upper bound is total correlation, whose noisy parity total correlation example shows why separate pairwise comparisons need not find all the dependence.

Information entropy OurBigBook.com
Cross-entropy measures the average logarithmic loss incurred when outcomes follow one probability distribution P, but a model assigns probabilities using another probability distribution Q. For a finite alphabet, write their probability mass functions as pi​ and qi​. With base-two logarithms,
H(P,Q)=−∑i:pi​>0​pi​log2​qi​=EP​[−log2​q(X)].

The expectation is under the true or stipulated source law P, rather than the model Q. Terms with pi​=0 contribute nothing. If pi​>0 but qi​=0 for any outcome, the cross-entropy is +∞: the model rules out an event that can occur. The result is measured in bits; natural logarithms give nats.
The useful identity is cross-entropy equals entropy plus relative entropy:
H(P,Q)=H(P)+DKL​(P∥Q).​
(113)
The source's information entropy H(P) is the baseline uncertainty. The Kullback-Leibler divergence is the extra average cost of a mismatched model, with the true law first and model second. Thus optimizing Q for a fixed P reduces the mismatch, rather than changing the source's own uncertainty. For finite alphabets, the minimum is H(P), attained exactly at Q=P.
Take a three-symbol source with P=(1/2,1/4,1/4). A matched binary prefix code assigns A↦0, B↦10, C↦11, with lengths (1,2,2). A mismatched prefix code instead assigns A↦10, B↦11, C↦0, with lengths (2,2,1), corresponding to Q=(1/4,1/4,1/2). Both prefix codes decode exactly, but the most common symbol is shorter in the matched code. Under the same source P,
H(P)H(P,Q)DKL​(P∥Q)​=21​⋅1+41​⋅2+41​⋅2=23​,=21​⋅2+41​⋅2+41​⋅1=47​,=21​log2​2+41​log2​1+41​log2​(1/2)=41​.​
(114)
The mismatched code costs an extra (1/4) bit per source symbol on average. No information is lost; the penalty is inefficient representation of this source. The mismatch penalty in lossless coding explains when this coding interpretation is exact.
Cross-entropy is also useful when evaluating a predictive distribution. A report that places tiny probability on the realized outcome receives a large logarithmic loss, even when it usually predicts the most common outcome correctly. The loss convention is the negative of the reward convention in the logarithmic scoring rule. Its expected loss is uniquely minimized by the correct probability distribution, making it a strictly proper scoring rule. Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation by Tilmann Gneiting and others treats this connection in §3.1, Example 3; its discussion uses rewards, so the signs are reversed for the losses here.[ref]
I. J. Good's Rational Decisions by I. J. Good appeared in 1952. Its published summary describes a method for encouraging accurate probability estimates and a connection with information theory. Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation by Tilmann Gneiting and others traces the logarithmic scoring rule at least as far back as this 1952 paper.[ref]

The unit is the bit. This is the smallest information content of any possible outcome: it records the easiest outcome to predict, whereas Shannon entropy averages information content over all outcomes. A normalized countable probability mass function has an attained positive maximum, so H∞​(X) is finite even when Shannon entropy is infinite. Outcomes of zero probability cannot minimize the surprise and are omitted from the minimum; including extra impossible symbols changes neither quantity.[ref]
Suppose someone knows the probability mass function but receives no observation correlated with X, and must name exactly one outcome. Naming x succeeds with probability px​, so naming a most likely outcome is optimal:

(133)
Tied maxima give equally good guesses. Randomizing independently among guesses cannot improve success: if the guess has probability mass function qx​, its success probability is ∑x​qx​px​≤pmax​∑x​qx​=pmax​. This is the simplest instance of maximum a posteriori decoding. The identity gives min-entropy an operational meaning: H∞​(X)≥k bits means every single guess succeeds with probability at most 2−k, under these information assumptions.[ref]
For an exact analytical example on symbols A,B,C,D,E, compare the two probability mass functions
u=(1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4,0),b=(1/2,1/8,1/8,1/8,1/8).

(135)

For the discrete uniform distribution on m possible outcomes, H∞​=log2​m bits and the best single guess succeeds with probability 1/m. A certain outcome has H∞​=0 and success probability one. Thus min-entropy is useful when a common outcome could defeat an attempt to make outputs unpredictable, even if rare alternatives raise Shannon entropy.
For cryptography, this unconditional calculation alone does not certify security: an observer might know X already. If a report Y=X reveals a uniform four-outcome source, its unconditional min-entropy remains 2 bits but guessing after the report succeeds with probability one. For finite classical reports, the appropriate success calculation uses conditional probabilities and maximum a posteriori decoding:
pguess​(X∣Y)=∑y:pY​(y)>0​pY​(y)maxx​P(X=x∣Y=y).
(136)
The conditional entropy H(X∣Y) instead averages remaining surprise. A security argument must specify the observer's information and the protocol's required guarantee; neither unconditional min-entropy nor Shannon entropy supplies those assumptions.

At q=1, both are zero; the four impossible alternatives contribute nothing. For every 1/5<q<1, the probability mass function is nonuniform on its possible outcomes and the gap is strictly positive.

Equality holds exactly for a discrete uniform distribution on the possible outcomes. Thus Shannon entropy alone supplies a lower bound on optimal success, not the upper bound needed to promise that every guess is unlikely. Shannon's source coding theorem concerns average compression under its hypotheses, while min-entropy answers the single-guess question directly. The two quantities serve different tasks even when both are expressed in bits.

Huffman coding

Words: 2k Articles: 13
Information theory OurBigBook.com
Huffman coding makes frequent symbols cheap to store by giving them short codewords, while allowing rare symbols longer codewords. For a known probability distribution on a finite alphabet with at least two positive-probability symbols, binary Huffman coding constructs a prefix code minimizing expected codeword length among binary prefix codes that encode one source symbol at a time. The objective is an average under that probability distribution; it does not promise to shorten every message. Encoder and decoder must agree on the resulting Huffman code. [ref]
The construction grows a binary tree from its leaves towards its root of a tree. Start with one leaf per symbol, weighted by its probability. Repeatedly join the two currently smallest weights beneath a new parent in a rooted tree, whose weight is their sum, and replace the pair by that subtree. Include newly formed subtrees when choosing the next pair. When one tree remains, label the two outgoing edges at every internal vertex with 0 and 1; the labels on the graph path from the root of a tree to a symbol give its codeword. This is a greedy algorithm: each step makes a locally cheapest merge, yet the result is an optimal prefix code.
For a concrete example, use probabilities pA​=0.4, pB​=0.3, pC​=0.2, pD​=0.1. First join D and C, creating weight 0.3. The remaining weights are 0.3 for B, 0.3 for the CD subtree, and 0.4 for A. Join the two 0.3 weights to make 0.6, then join A with that 0.6 subtree to make 1. The merge weights are therefore 0.3,0.6,1. Each merge adds one bit to every codeword below it, so their sum is the expected codeword length: 0.3+0.6+1=1.9 bits per source symbol. The diagram fixes the edge labels to produce the Huffman code used below.
The useful insight is that choosing short codewords is a resource allocation problem: the prefix code condition constrains the available codeword lengths through the Kraft inequality. Huffman coding solves this one-symbol problem exactly for the supplied probability distribution. For repeated emissions of a memoryless classical information source, the same Huffman code can be applied symbol by symbol. More general compression can exploit dependencies or encode groups of symbols; the one-symbol optimality statement does not compare all such methods.

Huffman code

Words: 395 Articles: 1
Huffman coding OurBigBook.com
A Huffman code is the prefix code returned by Huffman coding; the algorithm chooses a code tree, while the code specifies the actual symbol-to-codeword assignment. For the probability distribution (0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1) in symbol order A,B,C,D, the illustrated binary tree gives
c(A)=0,c(B)=10,c(C)=110,c(D)=111.
(147)
The codeword lengths are 1,2,3,3. This is a prefix code because no complete codeword is an initial segment of another complete codeword. Thus a decoder can start at the root of a tree, follow one edge per bit, emit a symbol on reaching its leaf, then restart at the root of a tree. In particular, 011010111 splits as 0 | 110 | 10 | 111 and decodes to A,C,B,D. No separators are transmitted: the leaf tells the decoder where a codeword ends.
The expected codeword length is
L(c)=∑x​px​∣c(x)∣=0.4⋅1+0.3⋅2+0.2⋅3+0.1⋅3=1.9
(148)
bits per source symbol. Four symbols would require 2 bits each if all codewords had the same length, so this Huffman code saves 0.1 bit per symbol on average, or 5% of that fixed-length payload. A particular message can grow: A,C,B,D uses nine bits here instead of eight. These lengths count the encoded symbols only; transmitting a code description or message framing can add further cost.
The Kraft inequality is saturated by this Huffman code:
2−1+2−2+2−3+2−3=1.
(149)
Its Shannon entropy is
H(X)=−∑x​px​log2​px​≈1.846439
(150)
bits per symbol, slightly below the expected codeword length 1.9. The entropy lower bound for prefix codes applies to every binary prefix code for this probability distribution. It need not be attainable with integer codeword lengths for individual symbols; Huffman coding reaches the best mean within that class. [ref]

Ties can also change the lengths themselves. For a second probability distribution (0.4,0.2,0.2,0.2), first merge C,D to weight 0.4. The next merge can join B with either A or the CD subtree, since both have weight 0.4. Joining B with A permits A↦00,B↦01,C↦10,D↦11, with all lengths 2. Joining B with the CD subtree permits A↦0,B↦10,C↦110,D↦111, with lengths 1,2,3,3. Both are optimal prefix codes with expected codeword length 2: for the latter, 0.4⋅1+0.2⋅2+0.2⋅3+0.2⋅3=2. Tie choices can change the code tree without changing the minimum mean.

Huffman sibling property

Words: 524 Articles: 2
Huffman coding OurBigBook.com
For a finite source alphabet of n≥2 symbols with positive weights wx​, choose any two least weights, breaking ties arbitrarily. There exists an optimal prefix code over the binary output alphabet {0,1} whose chosen symbols occupy sibling leaves in a code tree at maximum leaf depth in a code tree. Weights may be counts or probabilities: dividing every weight by W=∑x​wx​ gives the same minimizers. The existence statement is what makes the first merge of Huffman coding safe. It does not say that every optimal prefix code already has the chosen pair together.[ref]
An exchange makes the idea tangible. Take probabilities (pA​,pB​,pC​,pD​)=(0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1). The prefix code D↦0, B↦10, C↦110, A↦111 has expected codeword length 2.5 bits. Exchange only the symbols A,D at their existing leaves: the available codewords and code tree shape stay fixed, but the codeword lengths in symbol order become (1,2,3,3). The new expected codeword length is 1.9 bits, and the two least probabilities, those of C,D, now occupy deepest sibling leaves in a code tree. The saving is (0.4−0.1)(3−1)=0.6 bit per source symbol.
Here is the short proof outline. An optimal prefix code with positive weights has a full binary tree as its code tree: suppressing a vertex with only one child shortens every codeword in that subtree and strictly reduces cost. A deepest leaf therefore has a leaf as its sibling, giving the deepest sibling property of an optimal prefix code. Put the two chosen least weights at these positions by successive exchanges of leaf labels. Moving a weight a from leaf depth in a code tree d to a deepest position D≥d, occupied by b≥a, changes the weighted sum by
ΔC=aD+bd−(ad+bD)=(a−b)(D−d)≤0.
(151)
Fix one chosen weight there, then move the other into the neighbouring deepest position; if it is already there, no exchange is needed. The prefix code condition survives because the set of codewords is unchanged. Starting from an optimal prefix code, the cost cannot decrease below the minimum, so these exchanges preserve optimality. Strictly unequal weights at unequal depths would give a strict decrease, explaining probability monotonicity of optimal prefix-code lengths. Equal weights or equal depths allow cost-neutral exchanges. [ref]
