Here the source alphabet is finite, has n≥2 symbols, and has px​>0 for every symbol; each source symbol receives one codeword over the binary output alphabet {0,1}. Its code tree puts the symbols at leaves. Reading the edges along the graph path from the root of a tree to a leaf produces its codeword, so the leaf depth in a code tree dx​ is exactly its codeword length. Thus
L(c)=∑x​px​dx​,L∗(p)=minc a binary prefix code​L(c).
(153)
For unnormalized positive weights, minimize C(T)=∑x​wx​dx​ instead; the corresponding expected codeword length is C(T)/∑x​wx​. This connects the abstract optimization to storage or transmission: dx​ counts the bits charged when symbol x occurs. Huffman coding attains this minimum; the Huffman sibling property and Huffman sibling contraction explain why. [ref]
For (pA​,pB​,pC​,pD​)=(0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1), a balanced code tree charges every symbol two bits, giving L=2. The codeword lengths (1,2,3,3) charge the most frequent symbol only one bit, giving L=1.9. The choice concerns weighted cost, not just the greatest codeword length: increasing that maximum from two to three can improve the average.
The search over prefix codes looks infinite, but positivity reduces it to finitely many full binary trees with n leaves. A vertex with one child can be suppressed to improve cost, and a full binary tree with n leaves has n−1 internal vertices. There are consequently finitely many such shapes and symbol assignments, so the minimum exists. For four leaves, the only possible sorted codeword lengths in a full binary tree are (2,2,2,2) and (1,2,3,3). Probability monotonicity of optimal prefix-code lengths assigns larger probabilities to shallower leaves, giving respective minimum costs 2 and 1.9 in this example. This is an independent small-instance check of the Huffman code.
These hypotheses matter. With zero weights, suppressing a subtree carrying only zero weight need not strictly improve cost, so an optimal prefix code need not have a full binary tree. A one-symbol source raises the convention of whether an empty codeword is allowed. Both cases are outside the original statement here. Encoding groups of symbols changes the source alphabet and the optimization problem; the minimum here concerns one source symbol per codeword.

Leaf depth in a code tree (dx​=∣c(x)∣)

Words: 39
Optimal prefix code OurBigBook.com
The number of edges on the graph path from the root of a tree to the leaf for symbol x in a code tree. The root of a tree has depth zero. Each edge contributes one bit to a binary codeword, so this depth equals the codeword length; weighting these depths by probabilities gives expected codeword length.

Balancing exchange for a uniform optimal prefix code

Words: 67
Optimal prefix code OurBigBook.com
For an equiprobable source, an optimal binary prefix tree has leaf depths differing by at most one. If one leaf has depth t and a deepest sibling pair has depth s≥t+2, split the shallow leaf into two children and collapse the deep pair into its parent. The number of leaves is unchanged and their total depth decreases by s−t−1>0, contradicting optimality.
// Target: probability-and-statistics.bigb

Expected codeword length (L(c))

Words: 17
Optimal prefix code OurBigBook.com
For a source symbol X and a code c, the expected codeword length is
L(c)=E[∣c(X)∣]=∑x​P(X=x)∣c(x)∣.
(154)

Probability monotonicity of optimal prefix-code lengths

Words: 37
Optimal prefix code OurBigBook.com
If symbols of probabilities pi​>pj​ have codeword lengths li​ and lj​ in an optimal prefix code, then li​≤lj​. Otherwise, exchanging their codewords preserves the prefix property and changes the expected length by
(pi​−pj​)(lj​−li​)<0,
(155)
contradicting optimality.

Deepest sibling property of an optimal prefix code

Words: 64
Optimal prefix code OurBigBook.com
Every optimal binary prefix code has two codewords of maximal length that differ only in their final bit. Indeed, choose a deepest leaf in the prefix tree. If its sibling were not a codeword, maximality of the depth would make that sibling subtree empty, so the chosen word could be shortened by deleting its final bit. This would preserve prefix-freeness and reduce expected length.

Nonunique optimal prefix code

Words: 322
Optimal prefix code OurBigBook.com
An optimal prefix code can be nonunique in several different senses. Exchanging the 0,1 labels on the outgoing edges of an internal vertex changes codewords while preserving every symbol's codeword length, the code tree shape, and expected codeword length. This freedom exists even with strictly unequal probabilities. Exchanging equal-probability symbols between leaves also preserves expected codeword length; if their leaf depths in a code tree differ, their individual codeword lengths change, though the set of leaf depths does not. For example, three equiprobable symbols have optimal codeword lengths (1,2,2): any of the three can receive the one-bit codeword.[ref]
Ties between weights of entire subtrees during Huffman coding can go further and change the code tree shape and its collection of codeword lengths. Take (pA​,pB​,pC​,pD​)=(0.4,0.2,0.2,0.2) and first merge C,D, creating weight 0.4. Next, B of weight 0.2 can merge either with A or with the CD subtree, both of weight 0.4. The two resulting prefix codes are
balancedunequal depths​c(A)000​c(B)0110​c(C)10110​c(D)11111​L(c)22​​
(156)
For the second prefix code, L=0.4⋅1+0.2⋅2+0.2⋅3+0.2⋅3=2 bits. Both merge sequences add weights 0.4,0.6,1, whose sum is 2. Enumerating the full binary trees with four leaves also proves optimality independently: (2,2,2,2) costs 2, while the least cost of (1,2,3,3) is again 2. The two code trees cannot be obtained from each other merely by relabelling leaves or exchanging edge labels: their collections of leaf depths in a code tree differ.
The quantifier in the Huffman sibling property is visible here too. Choose B,C as two least-probability symbols. In the displayed balanced optimal prefix code, they are not sibling leaves in a code tree. Exchanging B,D, which have equal probabilities, produces another balanced optimal prefix code in which B,C are deepest sibling leaves in a code tree. Thus the proof supplies an optimal representative with the chosen pair together. It does not force that labelling on every optimum. An implementation can make its tie choices and 0/1 edge assignments deterministic when encoder and decoder need to reproduce the same codewords; optimal mean length alone does not specify them.

Huffman codeword length bounds

Words: 20
Huffman coding OurBigBook.com
For a largest binary-symbol probability p1​, p1​<1/3 prevents a length-one word, while p1​>2/5 forces one in a Huffman tree.

Bernoulli source

Words: 13
Information theory OurBigBook.com
A Bernoulli information source emits independent symbols with one fixed probability distribution.

Entropy rate (h(X)=limn→∞​H(X1​,…,Xn​)/n)

Words: 695 Articles: 6
Information theory OurBigBook.com
The entropy rate measures average new uncertainty per emitted symbol of a stochastic process. Predictability from earlier symbols can make this much smaller than the information entropy of one symbol. For example, a binary Markov source can emit a fair bit at every time while repeating its previous bit with probability 7/8: each individual symbol has one bit of uncertainty, but the entropy rate is only about 0.544 bits per symbol.
For a finite alphabet source X=(X1​,X2​,…), define
h(X)=limn→∞​nH(X1​,…,Xn​)​
(157)
when the limit exists. Base-two logarithms give bits per symbol. Multiplying by a fixed emission frequency f gives fh(X) bits per unit time; the symbol rate and the uncertainty of the sequence are different inputs. A strictly stationary process on a finite alphabet always has an entropy rate, equal to its conditional entropy rate.[ref]
For an independent and identically distributed source, the chain rule for information entropy gives H(X1​,…,Xn​)=nH(X1​), hence h(X)=H(X1​). With dependence, conditioning reduces entropy and makes the past useful. The examples under Markov information source show this benefit using exact finite-block calculations.

Conditional entropy rate (limn→∞​H(Xn​∣X1​,…,Xn−1​))

Words: 100
Entropy rate OurBigBook.com
For a strictly stationary process on a finite alphabet, put a1​=H(X1​) and an​=H(Xn​∣X1​,…,Xn−1​) for n≥2. Each an​ is the average remaining uncertainty in the next symbol after its history is known. More history can improve prediction, so this sequence is nonincreasing:
an+1​=H(Xn+1​∣X1​,…,Xn​)≤H(Xn+1​∣X2​,…,Xn​)=an​.
(158)
The inequality uses conditioning reduces entropy; the last equality uses strict stationarity. Nonnegative an​ therefore have a limit. By the chain rule for information entropy,
nH(X1​,…,Xn​)​=n1​∑j=1n​aj​.
(159)
The Cesàro mean converges to the same limit, proving the equality with the entropy rate. This is a statement about average information entropy. A constant almost-sure limit of the realized information content requires the further hypotheses in the Shannon-McMillan-Breiman theorem; stationarity without ergodicity in an information source explains the distinction.

Entropy rate and coding length

Words: 246
Entropy rate OurBigBook.com
Consider a binary Markov source with fair initial bit and flip probability q=1/8. Its exact n-symbol information entropy is Hn​=1+(n−1)h2​(1/8). At n=16,
H16​≃9.15346665 bits,H16​/16≃0.57209167 bits per symbol.
(160)
This includes the uncertainty of the initial bit; the entropy rate itself is h2​(1/8)≃0.54356444 bits per symbol. The finite-block difference is (1−h2​(1/8))/n.
For any finite block distribution, the entropy lower bound for prefix codes gives expected codeword length Ln​≥Hn​, while Shannon coding achieves Ln​<Hn​+1. These bounds apply to each block as one source symbol, without requiring consecutive blocks to be independent. Here Huffman coding on all 216 possible 16-symbol words gives the independently calculated value L16​≃9.19511361 bits per block, or 0.57469460 bits per symbol. The noninteger value is an expected value; each actual codeword has an integer length. As the block length grows, the prefix code bounds squeeze Ln​/n towards the entropy rate when an optimal code is used.
An entropy rate below one does not allow every word to fit into a shorter fixed binary word with zero error. For 0<q<1, all 2n binary words are possible, so an injective fixed-length code needs at least n bits. Compression instead exploits variable codeword lengths, or the vanishing-error convention in reliable source encoding at a rate. These are different guarantees.

Shannon's block-entropy approximations

Words: 79
Entropy rate OurBigBook.com
In A Mathematical Theory of Communication by Claude Shannon, Claude Shannon compares block uncertainty per symbol, denoted GN​, with conditional uncertainty given the preceding symbols, denoted FN​. Theorems 5 and 6 connect both decreasing approximations to the source's limiting uncertainty. He uses symbol statistics at increasing block lengths to expose structure missed by single-letter counts.[ref] The fair marginal bits of the binary Markov source provide a small exact example of that distinction.

Reliable source encoding at a rate

Words: 88 Articles: 1
Entropy rate OurBigBook.com
A source is reliably encodable at rate r if there are block encoders with at most 2nr outputs and corresponding decoders whose probability of reconstructing the first n source symbols incorrectly tends to zero as n→∞.

Strong converse for fixed-rate source coding

Words: 51
Reliable source encoding at a rate OurBigBook.com
For a finite-alphabet IID source of entropy H, fixed-length block codes of rate R<H have reconstruction success probability tending to zero. At most 2nR strings can be correctly reconstructed. Their typical probability is at most 2nR2−n(H−δ), and the atypical probability tends to zero; choose 0<δ<H−R.

Entropy rate OurBigBook.com
For a source (Xn​) and fixed positive integer N, form the block source Yi​=(X(i−1)N+1​,…,XiN​). Whenever the original information rate h exists, the blocked source has information rate Nh, because
m1​H(Y1​,…,Ym​)=NmN1​H(X1​,…,XmN​).

Markov information source

Words: 561 Articles: 4
Information theory OurBigBook.com
A Markov information source uses a stationary finite Markov chain to emit symbols. The emitted symbol can be a function of the state. If it does not identify that state, the observed sequence need not itself be a Markov chain. The examples here use a fully observed Markov source, which makes the next-symbol uncertainty directly computable from the transition matrix.

Fully observed Markov source

Words: 513 Articles: 3
Markov information source OurBigBook.com
Each emitted symbol identifies the state of a stationary finite Markov chain. Here the alphabet is the state space itself. Its transition matrix P and stationary distribution π determine the entropy rate of a fully observed Markov source.

Entropy rate of a fully observed Markov source (h=−∑i​πi​∑j​Pij​log2​Pij​)

Words: 112
Fully observed Markov source OurBigBook.com
For a fully observed Markov source, the Markov property makes the last state sufficient for the next symbol's conditional distribution. With stationary distribution π, the conditional entropy is therefore
h=H(X2​∣X1​)=−∑i​πi​∑j​Pij​log2​Pij​,
(162)
using 0log2​0=0. The chain rule for information entropy gives the exact finite-block identity
H(X1​,…,Xn​)=H(π)+(n−1)h.
(163)
Dividing by n proves the displayed entropy rate. The weighting by πi​ matters: rows with high uncertainty contribute in proportion to how often their states occur.
For an original asymmetric example, take
P=(7/83/8​1/85/8​),π=(3/4,1/4).
(164)
The equality πP=π verifies the stationary distribution. The single-symbol information entropy is h2​(1/4)≃0.81127812, whereas
h=43​h2​(1/8)+41​h2​(3/8)≃0.64628183 bits per symbol.​
(165)
This formula describes observed states. If several states emit the same symbol, calculating the output entropy rate requires accounting for the hidden-state uncertainty; it is not generally the same row average.

Binary Markov source

Words: 379 Articles: 1
Fully observed Markov source OurBigBook.com
Take the alphabet {0,1}, fair initial bit X1​, and transition matrix
P=(1−qq​q1−q​),0≤q≤1.
(166)
The stationary distribution is (1/2,1/2). Every emitted symbol is a fair bit, while the next symbol flips the previous one with probability q. For q<1/2, repeating the previous symbol is the better one-step prediction; for q>1/2, predicting its opposite is better. The resulting minimum next-symbol error probability is min(q,1−q), compared with 1/2 when no history is used.
Given either state, the next-symbol information entropy is h2​(q). Thus
H(Xn​)=1,H(Xn​∣X1​,…,Xn−1​)=h2​(q)(n≥2),h(X)=h2​(q).​
(167)
At q=1/8, the best next-symbol prediction succeeds with probability 7/8, and the entropy rate is about 0.54356444 bits per symbol. The adjacent symbols share mutual information I(X1​;X2​)=1−h2​(q)≃0.45643556 bits. This is useful structure even though the single-symbol counts reveal no bias.
At q=0, the random initial bit is repeated forever; at q=1, it alternates forever. Both have H(X1​,…,Xn​)=1 and zero entropy rate. At q=1/2, the symbols are independent and identically distributed fair bits, giving entropy rate one. Zero rate therefore need not mean that the initial choice was deterministic.
Innovations in a binary Markov source (Zn​=Xn​⊕Xn−1​)
Words: 133
Binary Markov source OurBigBook.com
Generate the binary Markov source by taking independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables Z2​,Z3​,… of parameter q, independent of a fair initial bit, and setting Xn​=Xn−1​⊕Zn​. Here ⊕ is exclusive or. Each Zn​ is the unpredictable flip decision.
The transformation between (X1​,…,Xn​) and (X1​,Z2​,…,Zn​) is a bijection. It preserves information entropy, so
H(X1​,…,Xn​)=H(X1​,Z2​,…,Zn​)=1+(n−1)h2​(q).
(168)
Sending the initial bit and encoding the innovation sequence describes every source word exactly. This does not by itself specify a practical compressor, but it identifies the uncertainty which a prefix code or other lossless source coding method must handle.
For a word with k flips among its n−1 transitions,
P(X1​=x1​,…,Xn​=xn​)=21​qk(1−q)n−1−k.
(169)
There are 2(kn−1​) such words: choose the initial bit and the flip positions. At q=1/8 and n=16, each constant word has probability (1/2)(7/8)15≃0.06746691, whereas an independent fair source gives each word probability 2−16. Equal marginal probabilities plainly do not imply equal word probabilities.

Asymptotic equipartition property (−n−1log2​P(Xn)→H(X1​))

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Information theory OurBigBook.com
The asymptotic equipartition property explains why a long message from a source can usually be described using its information entropy per symbol. Individual messages can have very different probabilities, but the messages carrying almost all the total probability have similar logarithmic costs per symbol. The Bernoulli typical-set example makes the distinction between an individual message and a large collection explicit.
For independent and identically distributed random variables X1​,X2​,… on a finite alphabet, let p be their probability mass function and H=E[−log2​p(X1​)]. Then
−n1​log2​P(X1​,…,Xn​)⟶Halmost surely.​
(170)
Here P(X1​,…,Xn​) means the probability mass of the realized word, evaluated under the source law. The product rule for independent random variables turns its information content into a sum:
−n1​log2​P(X1​,…,Xn​)=n1​∑j=1n​[−log2​p(Xj​)].
(171)
The strong law of large numbers gives the limit. Zero-probability symbols do not occur; on the positive-probability support of a finite alphabet, these information costs are finite. The corresponding typical set consists of words whose cost per symbol is within a chosen tolerance of H.
For a strictly stationary process with a finite alphabet, the constant-limit extension requires ergodicity. The Shannon-McMillan-Breiman theorem then replaces the one-symbol information entropy with the information rate. Stationarity without ergodicity in an information source shows why stationarity alone is insufficient.[ref]

Bernoulli typical-set example (p=1/4,H=h2​(1/4)≈0.811278)

Words: 433 Articles: 2
Asymptotic equipartition property OurBigBook.com
Take an IID random variable source of bits with P(Xj​=1)=1/4. Its binary entropy is
H=h2​(1/4)=−41​log2​41​−43​log2​43​≈0.811278 bits per symbol.
(172)
A word of length n containing k ones has probability (1/4)k(3/4)n−k. Its information content per symbol is
n(k)​=log2​34​+nk​log2​3.
(173)
Thus weakly typical sequences for this biased source have k/n near 1/4. With tolerance ε=0.1 bits per symbol, the exact condition is
​nk​−41​​≤log2​30.1​.
(174)
For n=40, this includes exactly k=8,9,10,11,12. There are (k40​) words with each count: a type class with that many possible orderings. Summing the counts and their probability masses gives
∣T0.1(40)​∣=9096659013,P(T0.1(40)​)≈0.638912.​
(175)
These are fewer than one percent of the 240 possible words, yet they carry nearly 64 percent of the probability. The most likely individual word is all zeros, with probability (3/4)40≈1.006×10−5; it is outside this typical set. No contradiction is involved: the type classes near ten ones each contain many more individual words.

Typical-set concentration for a biased coin

Words: 133
Bernoulli typical-set example OurBigBook.com
The count Kn​ has binomial distribution with mean n/4 and variance 3n/16. The information content per symbol is an affine function of Kn​/n, so its variance is
Var(n(Kn​)​)=16n3(log2​3)2​.
(176)
Chebyshev's inequality therefore gives the finite-sample lower bound
P(Tε(n)​)≥max(0,1−16nε23(log2​3)2​).
(177)
The bound is often loose, but it proves that every fixed positive tolerance eventually captures nearly all the probability. Direct summation of the binomial distribution's probability masses gives P(T0.1(640)​)≈0.999779. A finite sample does not need to have a nearly full typical set: the 40-symbol example above captures only about 0.639.

Typical-set indexing example (Ln​=⌈log2​(∣Tε(n)​∣+1)⌉)

Words: 112
Bernoulli typical-set example OurBigBook.com
The typical sequence theorem turns a probability concentration into a coding construction. Assign one binary number index to each weakly typical sequence, plus a reserved index for every word outside the set. The decoder recovers every typical word exactly; the reserved index has one predetermined output. The block code uses
Ln​=⌈log2​(∣Tε(n)​∣+1)⌉
(178)
bits and has reconstruction-error probability at most 1−P(Tε(n)​).
For this example and ε=0.1, n=40 needs 34 bits but permits error up to about 0.3611. At n=640, 570 bits suffice and the error bound is about 0.0002215. These are existence calculations for an explicitly enumerated collection, rather than claims about an efficient practical encoder. The reduction comes from protecting the whole high-probability collection, rather than just its single most likely member.

Stationarity without ergodicity in an information source

Words: 142
Asymptotic equipartition property OurBigBook.com
Choose one of two regimes once, with equal probability: a source of independent and identically distributed random variables with one-bit probability 1/10, or one with one-bit probability 1/2. Keep the chosen regime forever. The resulting source is a strictly stationary process, because shifting a block does not change either component law. It is not an ergodic stationary process: its limiting empirical frequency identifies the regime.
The source's information rate is
21​h2​(1/10)+21​h2​(1/2)≈0.734498.
(179)
Conditioning on the single regime bit changes any block's information entropy by at most one bit, so dividing by the block length proves this rate. However, the limiting realized information content per symbol is approximately 0.468996 in the first regime and one in the second. The alternative component's likelihood ratio decays exponentially along a typical path from the chosen component, at a rate given by the positive relative entropy between the two Bernoulli distributions. The mixture therefore has two possible pathwise limits, not one limit equal to the averaged information rate.

Shannon's typical-message formulation

Words: 77
Asymptotic equipartition property OurBigBook.com
In A Mathematical Theory of Communication by Claude Shannon (1948, section 7), Claude Shannon explains that the common symbol counts in a long independent message make its negative logarithmic probability approximately the message length times the source entropy. Theorem 3 separates an exceptional collection of small total probability from messages with this normalized information cost; Theorem 4 relates the number needed to accumulate a fixed probability to the entropy. The finite-state source setting matters to the historical statement.[ref]

Typical set (Tε(n)​)

Words: 308 Articles: 4
Asymptotic equipartition property OurBigBook.com
For an IID source, the epsilon-typical set consists of words un satisfying ∣−(1/n)logp(un)−H(U)∣≤ε. Its probability tends to one, and its cardinality is at most 2n(H(U)+ε).

Typical sequence theorem (P(Tε(n)​)→1,∣Tε(n)​∣≤2n(H+ε))

Words: 129
Typical set OurBigBook.com
For a memoryless classical information source, the typical set consists of positive-probability words with ∣−(1/n)log2​p(un)−H(U)∣≤ε. The weak law of large numbers applied to −log2​p(Uj​) proves its probability tends to one. Every typical word has probability between 2−n(H+ε) and 2−n(H−ε). Summing the lower bound gives the displayed cardinality upper bound; if the set has probability at least 1−δ, summing the upper bound gives cardinality at least (1−δ)2n(H−ε).
To compress at any rate R>H(U), choose 0<ε<R−H(U), assign one fixed-length binary index to each typical word, and reserve one additional index for all atypical words. At most ⌈nR⌉ bits suffice for all large n. Decoding inverts the typical-word indices and makes an arbitrary output for the reserved index. The reconstruction error is at most the probability of the atypical set and tends to zero.

Typical set OurBigBook.com
For an IID random variable source with probability mass function p, a word xn is weakly typical when ∣−(1/n)log2​p(xn)−H(X)∣≤ε. It has probability on the scale 2−nH(X). The weak law of large numbers makes the typical set probable, but does not make every word in it representative: for a uniform source every possible word is weakly typical.

For a finite-alphabet IID random variable source, a strongly typical word has empirical symbol frequencies within the chosen tolerance of every p(x), and contains no zero-probability symbols. Lossless source coding encodes source messages so they can be recovered exactly. Shannon's source coding theorem relates its achievable average code length to information entropy.
